title: Westbrook City Council — Regular Meeting

blocks.x: Roll Call & President Pro Tem
Roll Call & Election of President Pro Tem
Discussion Summary
First meeting of 2026. Roll call: Councilors Shaughnessy, McCambridge, Chau, Turcotte, Faulkingham, and Rairdon answered present. That is six of seven members.
President Jennifer Munro was not named at roll call at all. The President and Vice President were absent.
Shaughnessy did join and vote by Zoom but did not preside. The Council elected Councilor Victor Chau as President Pro Tem, a temporary presiding officer, to run tonight's meeting.
Key Decisions
Victor Chau elected President Pro Tem by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Amy Faulkingham.
Action Items
None.
Mayor's Message
New City Administrator, Budget Good News & County Fiscal Watch
Discussion Summary
Mayor David Morse welcomed new City Administrator Angela Holmes to her first meeting in the role (sworn in the prior Friday).

Workers' compensation savings: the City's 2026 premium came in at $360,373. That is down sharply from $556,683 in 2025. The drop was driven by the experience-modification rate improving from 1.08 to 0.84.
The FY26 budget had set aside $645,000. This is a large favorable variance, meaning a gap between the budget and the actual cost, heading into next year's budget.

Cumberland County fiscal watch: if the County's federal contract covering Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees is terminated, the County budget would need to grow about 13.77% instead of about 5.37%. This is something to watch for the FY27 city budget.
Holiday tree pickup runs Dec. 29 – Jan. 12, with allowance for residents observing Orthodox Christmas (Jan. 6–7).
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken.
Action Items
None.
Trash Collection Crisis Over the Holidays
Discussion Summary
A Dec. 23–24 snowstorm caused Casella Waste to cancel routes. That week's collection was already shifted for Christmas, so no makeup day was available.

Casella told the City it would let residents drop off trash at its County Road facility all week. But when a resident tried to, staff at the gate turned him away. They said Westbrook wasn't part of their program.

Director Eric Dudley made calls up the chain and drove to the transfer station himself to get it resolved. Missed streets continued into the following week. The Wednesday, Dec. 31 route was so backed up that Casella brought employees in on their New Year's Day holiday to finish it.
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken; ongoing issue.
Action Items
Mayor has asked Eric Dudley to arrange a meeting with Casella leadership. The City has also asked legal counsel to review the contract — Assignee: Administration | Deadline: none set.

“The folks at the gate were told to not accept Westbrook trash... which is not what they had offered us and certainly not what we relayed to the general public as well as all of you... I find [that] completely unacceptable.”
blocks.cite: Director of Engineering & Public Services Eric Dudley

blocks.x: “I think that there — you cannot have a monopoly on a garbage [contract] that long... I think that we could be a little more creative in finding solutions to step away from that contract.”

Dudley said the City checked Waste Management as an alternative in 2020 and found it probably 30–40% more expensive. He said he doesn't know whether Waste Management currently runs automated curbside collection in Maine. He said the City is checking whether it can offer an option.
The City's relationship with Casella goes back 30+ years. The current 10-year contract began in 2020.

Public Comment (First)

Two kinds of public comment tonight. One was a resident previewing the Foster Street parking debate taken up later in New Business (see below). The other was four written letters read into the record. One was on Foster Street parking, and three were on a separate, more sensitive matter.
Carson Wood

A longtime resident who is now completely blind previewed his request for an accessible parking space positioned directly in front of his steps, not shifted toward Main Street as then drawn. See the full debate under Order 2026-01 below.
The Dory Schollberger / 12 Water Street Letters

The Council did not discuss these on the record. They are reproduced here because these are the public's own words on a contentious matter, not because any councilor or staff member responded to them tonight.
“Dory is a big part of this neighborhood... She has lived her whole life at this address... I am asking you to stop the eviction process and either sell her the land or give her a long-term rental.”
blocks.cite: Don Kelly, read by City Clerk Ellis Ledoux (on behalf of neighbor Don Kelly, for “Dory”)

blocks.x: “Your discussions have all been behind closed doors in executive session. There are no public records to indicate anything that is being discussed... Twelve Water Street has been a house lot for over sixty years. Why can it not continue as a house lot?”

“I urge the city to sell Dory the plot of land upon which her house stands. If it does not, it should at least compensate her the fair market value of her house, as is done by taking an eminent domain.”

Conley cited a Zillow estimate of $75,000 for the house without land. Peterson's letter said city records list a $78,015 replacement cost. The meeting later entered executive session, a closed, private session allowed by state law for certain topics, for “pending or contemplated litigation” with no further public detail. Readers should not assume this is the same matter without confirmation, but the timing and subject overlap is worth noting.
Orders of the Day — Second & Final Reading
Orders 2025-169, 170, 171 — Consent Block (Non-Union Pay Plan, Police Lateral-Hire Reimbursement, Highway Safety Grant Funds)

Order 2025-170, a $48,671 reimbursement to the City of South Portland for a lateral-hire officer's training costs (required by state law).
Order 2025-171 accepts $38,621.40 in Bureau of Highway Safety traffic-enforcement grant funds across six categories.

Order 2026-01 — Foster Street Parking
One reading only. This amends the Code of Ordinances (§310-71, §310-106), the City's collection of laws.

It removes the parking ban on the west side of Foster Street (the east side stays no-parking). It also lets the Police Chief or City Engineer designate, and later remove, accessible parking spaces citywide as needs change. That way a specific location is not hard-coded into the ordinance itself.

Carson Wood, a longtime 20 Foster St. resident who is now completely blind, asked for an accessible space directly in front of his steps. The space would let him manage trash cans, groceries, and service vehicles without using street parking he otherwise never relies on.
“What it needs to be starting at is at the end of [the porch post]... where I need a handicap spot is right in front of my steps... I don't need it up the street or down the street.”
The amendment attempt — Councilor Gary Rairdon
“I would like to make an amendment to have loading parking only, because that would serve for the servicing of 20 Foster Street... that would prevent cars from sitting there a long period of time.”
Rairdon argued a commercial-plates-only loading zone would still let service vehicles reach Wood's property. He said it would also discourage long-term parking and preserve room for fire apparatus.
Director Dudley clarified that loading zones legally require a commercial plate. That excludes an ordinary lawn-care worker's or plumber's personal vehicle, undercutting the idea in practice.
The amendment failed, 0–6. Rairdon's follow-up suggestion of general 2-hour parking in the same stretch also died for lack of a second.
Key Decisions

Order approved as written [1:04:02] 5–1, Gary Rairdon the lone dissent. Moved by Brian McCambridge, seconded by Anna Turcotte. For: Michael Shaughnessy, McCambridge, Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Victor Chau. Against: Rairdon.
Action Items

Director Dudley proposed meeting Carson Wood on-site before installing anything. He ruled out placing the space mid-stretch, which would eliminate other parking. He said it could return to the Council if no solution is reached — Assignee: Engineering & Public Services | Deadline: none set.

$24,405.50 for 50 rifle suppressors, paid through the Police Department's federal forfeiture funds. Police Captain Goldberg said they would help the department be “good neighbors” during range training. He said they would also serve as protective equipment for officers if ever deployed on the street. The packet memo cites hearing protection and less noise near the open-air range.
Key Decisions
Passed first reading (the first of two required votes), unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Anna Turcotte, seconded by Gary Rairdon.

$33,160.36 for a John Deere 2025R compact utility tractor and quick-hitch rotary broom.
